topic.title: the equal-bill friendship
topic.claim: The first time you earn more than a close friend, you start ordering cheaper when you eat with them.
topic.moment: dinner with a best friend after the salaries split

cover.headline: Earn more than your best friend, and you [start ordering cheaper].
cover.sub: Nobody told you to. You just did.

paragraphs: Earn more than your best friend, and you start ordering cheaper.
Same college. Same canteen. Same broke last week of every month.
Then the offer letters came, and one was double the other.
Now at dinner you scan the menu for the cheap side first. You say "I'm not that hungry." You pick the place near their office, not yours.
When the bill comes, you split it exactly. Never more, even though you could.
Because paying for both of you would say the thing out loud.
Friendships here run on being equals. The moment one of you is visibly doing better, everything gets managed so the other one doesn't feel it. Call it the equal-bill friendship.
And your friend knows. They notice you ordered the dal when you could have had anything.
And I don't think it's pity.
It's the most Indian kind of love: protecting someone's pride by pretending there's nothing to protect.
**You can afford the expensive dinner. What you can't afford is your friend noticing.**

end.send: Send to the friend you always split the bill with, exactly.
end.save: Read it before your next dinner with them.

claims.text: In Indian friendships built on equality, when one friend starts earning visibly more than the other, both friends manage spending and ordering choices (e.g., the higher earner orders cheaper, picks cheaper venues, splits bills exactly) so the gap isn't felt, producing a recognizable 'equal-bill friendship' pattern
claims.sentence: Earn more than your best friend, and you start ordering cheaper... Friendships here run on being equals. The moment one of you is visibly doing better, everything gets managed so the other one doesn't feel it. Call it the equal-bill friendship.

bce9490d64b212e65d625e869d6d40b80dfc7062.broken_premise: None. The post makes no falsifiable claim about how a product, price, fee, tax, law, contract or market works. Every load-bearing element is opinion or a generalization about everyday life: that higher earners order cheaper to hide the gap, that friendships 'run on being equals,' that the restraint is 'love protecting pride.' These are readings of motive and interpretations of a moment, which the brief explicitly excludes from falsification. The only mechanical claim — that friends can and do split a bill exactly down the middle — is plainly true and requires no external source.
bce9490d64b212e65d625e869d6d40b80dfc7062.actual_mechanism: Bill-splitting among peers is a pure social convention, not a priced or regulated transaction: a restaurant presents one total and diners choose any division (equal split, itemized, or one person treating), so 'splitting exactly' is always available and carries no fee or rule. Everything else the post asserts — the motive behind ordering the dal, the unspoken mutual awareness, the 'equal-bill friendship' label — is the writer's interpretation of behavior, not a factual mechanism that can be checked against a law, rate or contract.
